articles.title: Blackstone Bets $5B on Google TPUs in AI Compute Venture Worth Up to $25B
articles.subtitle: The JV puts Google's proprietary AI silicon on an off-balance-sheet capital structure for the first time.
articles.body_md:
**Blackstone** committed **$5B in equity** from its managed funds to a new joint venture with **Google** that will sell compute-as-a-service using Google Tensor Processing Units — announced May 18–20, 2026, the largest single private-capital commitment to a non-GPU AI compute platform to date. Total investment, including leverage, is projected at **up to $25B**, with the first **500 MW** of capacity targeted for online delivery in 2027.

The structure is architecturally distinct from every prior AI infrastructure deal. **KKR Helix** (Edition 12) and **AIP/Aligned Data Centers** (Edition 5) are NVIDIA GPU-centric compute platforms built around general-purpose hardware. The Blackstone/Google JV is purpose-built for TPU workloads: Google supplies hardware, software, and services, while Blackstone provides capital and data centre operations. **Benjamin Treynor Sloss** — co-founder of Google's Site Reliability Engineering discipline and former VP Engineering — leads the venture as CEO, embedding Google's operational credibility at the executive layer.

## The NVIDIA Hedge

For European infrastructure investors, three implications stand out. First, the venture validates that proprietary AI silicon — Google's TPU stack, purpose-built for TensorFlow and JAX workloads — can compete with NVIDIA CUDA as an enterprise compute standard. Second, the capital structure is a scalable template: Google operates data centres in Ireland (Dublin), Belgium, Netherlands, and Finland, each a potential European expansion vector. Third, Blackstone's sequential moves — a DC REIT IPO filing (Edition 10) and now this JV — confirm that the largest PE capital allocators are building cross-platform AI compute exposure rather than single-hardware bets.

The **$25B scale** puts this venture in the same tier as AIP's **$100B deployment target** (Edition 5) and KKR Helix's **$10B+ committed capital** (Edition 12). The difference is hardware specificity: Blackstone is now simultaneously long NVIDIA (via data centre REIT) and long Google TPU (via this JV), hedging the hardware standard question rather than resolving it.

In the next 12–18 months, watch whether the JV announces a European colocation partner for post-2027 expansion, whether Google names a Nordic or Dublin campus as the first international TPU-cloud site, and whether **Microsoft** or **Amazon** respond with analogous off-balance-sheet structures for their own proprietary AI chip programmes — Microsoft's Maia and Amazon's Trainium are the logical next candidates.
articles.summary: Blackstone committed $5B in equity to a new Google TPU compute-as-a-service venture with total investment projected up to $25B — the largest private-capital commitment to a non-GPU AI compute platform to date. The structure embeds Google hardware into a Blackstone capital and data centre infrastructure vehicle, with 500 MW of US capacity targeted by 2027 and European expansion as the key medium-term watch.

articles.title: Nscale's $790M Narvik Debt Package Makes Norway Europe's AI Compute Anchor
articles.subtitle: State export credit backing and 30,000 Rubin GPUs confirm Narvik as a replicable template for Nordic AI project finance.
articles.body_md:
**Nscale** secured a **$790M (€670M) infrastructure debt facility** for its Narvik AI campus on May 12, 2026, in a five-bank syndicate comprising **ABN AMRO, DNB, Eksfin** (the Norwegian Export Credit Agency), **Nordea**, and **SEB**. The base campus is **230 MW**, with an uncommitted accordion feature that can extend capacity to **520 MW**. Total capital committed to Narvik — across equity, term loans, and this facility — now exceeds **$4.2B**.

The single most significant data point is Eksfin's participation. Norway's state export credit agency does not typically participate in commercial data centre debt. Its inclusion signals that the Norwegian government has classified the Narvik campus as national industrial infrastructure — aligning the country's hydro power surplus with an AI compute strategy that carries de facto sovereign backing. **Microsoft**'s April 2026 commitment of **more than 30,000 NVIDIA Rubin GPUs** to the campus, targeted for H2 2027 delivery, de-risks demand for Nscale's most capital-intensive construction phase and confirms Narvik as the largest contracted GPU deployment at a single European-built campus.

## A Replicable Capital Template

The power economics underpin everything. Narvik is served by municipal hydropower at approximately **€0.03–0.04/kWh** — roughly one-eighth of UK industrial tariffs and one-sixth of the cost that prompted OpenAI to pause the Stargate UK deployment (Edition 6). At **230 MW**, the annual operating cost differential versus a comparable UK or Dublin campus runs to hundreds of millions of euros over a 10-year lease.

Nscale's capital structure is a template worth studying. The prior tranches — a **$2B Series C** (March 2026, led by **Aker ASA**) and a **$1.4B Delayed Draw Term Loan** (February 2026) — establish a layered project finance stack. The infrastructure debt facility converts what began as a venture-stage equity story into a conventional project finance structure anchored on sovereign-grade power supply and anchor hyperscaler offtake. That architecture is directly replicable at other Norwegian hydro locations and at Swedish sites with equivalent power economics.

In the next 12–18 months, watch the accordion drawdown timeline (the clearest signal of additional hyperscaler commitments beyond Microsoft), any **Aker ASA** secondary sell-down of its Series C position, and whether competing Nordic operators announce comparable debt syndication for greenfield AI campus projects in Sweden or Iceland.
articles.summary: Nscale closed a $790M infrastructure debt facility for its 230MW Narvik AI campus, with Norway's state export credit agency Eksfin joining a five-bank syndicate — confirming the project has sovereign-grade strategic backing. Microsoft's commitment of 30,000+ NVIDIA Rubin GPUs for H2 2027 delivery de-risks the demand side and makes Narvik the most heavily capitalised single European AI campus.

articles.title: Bain Capital's HSCALE Commits €2B to Milan — Non-FLAP Europe's Largest DC Bet
articles.subtitle: Two liquid-cooled campuses totalling 250MW confirm Milan as PE capital's preferred non-FLAP European hyperscale destination.
articles.body_md:
**HSCALE**, the hyperscale data centre platform jointly founded by **Bain Capital** and **Aquila Group** in 2025, has closed its second campus in **Settimo, Northwest Milan**, bringing total committed power capacity in the Milan area to **250 MW** and total capital commitment to over **€2B**. Both campuses are targeted for ready-for-service in **2028**. The same week, **Digital Realty** launched **BCN1**, its first Barcelona data centre, in the Sant Adrià de Besòs innovation district — together marking the most concentrated single-week capital commitment to Southern European digital infrastructure on record.

HSCALE was structured from inception as an EMEA platform targeting non-FLAP markets — Italy, Spain, and Poland — where the thesis is that better risk-adjusted returns are available than in congested Dublin, Amsterdam, or Frankfurt. The **liquid-cooled-first** architectural choice positions both Milan campuses for high-density AI training and inference workloads where cooling density directly affects customer economics. Both facilities are physically flexible enough to pivot to conventional air-cooled deployments, avoiding the stranding risk of single-architecture facilities.

## Italy's Grid Moment

The Settimo location is deliberate. It sits within an established European hyperscale corridor with proximity to **Alpine power transmission routes** — providing grid access that is materially harder and more expensive to secure in southern or eastern Italy. Italy's grid operator **Terna** has been accelerating large-user connection approvals through 2025–26 following government pressure to attract data centre investment; HSCALE's 2028 timeline is achievable if that acceleration holds.

The implied capital intensity — approximately **€8M per MW** across a 250 MW buildout — is consistent with European hyperscale greenfield benchmarks and signals that secondary-market DC assets command the same capital efficiency as FLAP-D projects when power supply is secured. Italy adds a dimension the Nordics cannot offer: proximity to Southern European content consumption and low-latency access to Mediterranean cable infrastructure, including the now state-controlled **TIM Sparkle** network. Digital Realty's simultaneous Barcelona launch reinforces the Southern European momentum — two distinct operators, two markets, in the same week.

In the next 12–18 months, watch for the first hyperscaler lease announcements for the Milan campuses, Italian grid connection timelines, and whether HSCALE announces a third European market — Poland is the most probable candidate based on the original EMEA platform thesis.
articles.summary: Bain Capital and Aquila Group's HSCALE platform has committed over €2B to two liquid-cooled hyperscale campuses in Northwest Milan totalling 250MW, both targeted for 2028 delivery — the largest single-operator PE commitment to Italian digital infrastructure on record. Digital Realty's simultaneous launch of its first Barcelona campus confirms non-FLAP Southern Europe is entering an active hyperscale buildout phase.

articles.title: Italy Reclaims Its Mediterranean Cable Gateway in €700M EC-Cleared Deal
articles.subtitle: Rome takes direct control of Italy's international subsea cable network as Mediterranean routing commands a new strategic premium.
articles.body_md:
The **European Commission** approved Italy's acquisition of **TIM Sparkle** on April 13, 2026, without antitrust conditions. The buyers are the **Italian Ministry of Economy and Finance (MEF)** and **Retelit** — itself owned by **Cellnex** (Spain) — in a **€700M deal including assumed debt**. TIM Sparkle is Italy's international submarine cable infrastructure: it operates the routing layer that connects European traffic to Gulf, African, and Asian markets via the Mediterranean.

The timing is deliberate and the strategic logic explicit. The Red Sea disruption (17 cables, no repair timeline — Edition 1) and Iran's formalisation of Hormuz cable permit requirements (Edition 12) have made Mediterranean routing materially more valuable as the alternative to Indo-Pacific transit. Italy, which sits at the geographic centre of Mediterranean cable geography, has moved to ensure that routing decisions and contract structures on that infrastructure are subject to Italian state oversight. The EC found no serious competition concerns — multiple alternative cable landing and backhaul operators exist — but the precedent set is more significant than the competition assessment.

## A Pattern Completing

TIM Sparkle is the third major European telecommunications strategic asset to come under state influence this year. France has intervened in **Altice SFR** (debt restructuring oversight); Germany has mandated **Huawei/ZTE removal** under binding bilateral agreements (Edition 10); Italy has now directly acquired its international cable gateway. In all three cases, European competition law has not blocked the intervention — a permissive precedent that five years ago would have been notable and is now unremarkable.

The Retelit co-ownership is a deliberate structural choice. **Cellnex**-owned Retelit brings operational telecom infrastructure expertise while keeping a private operator in the structure — a hybrid that signals Italy is not pursuing full renationalisation but strategic control with commercial discipline. The remaining hurdle is **US regulatory clearance** (OFAC/FCC), which **TIM** guided for **Q2 2026**; completion triggers a **TIM share buyback** as part of the ongoing financial restructuring that began with the NetCo separation.

In the next 12–18 months, watch whether MEF exercises strategic veto rights over Sparkle cable contracts with US hyperscalers, the timing and conditions of US regulatory clearance, and whether any other EU member state — France or Spain are the most probable — follows Italy's template for direct acquisition of strategic subsea infrastructure.
articles.summary: The European Commission cleared Italy's €700M acquisition of TIM Sparkle — the country's international submarine cable operator — by MEF and Cellnex-owned Retelit, without conditions. The deal gives Rome direct control of Mediterranean routing infrastructure as Red Sea and Hormuz disruptions have elevated the strategic value of alternative subsea corridors.

articles.title: €176B Will Flow Into European Data Centres by 2031. Grids Will Decide Where.
articles.subtitle: The industry's clearest statement yet: capital is abundant for European digital infrastructure, electricity grids are not.
articles.body_md:
The **European Data Centre Association (EDCA)** forecast **€176B in cumulative European data centre investment** from 2026 to 2031, announced in the week of May 19–23, 2026 — the deepest sustained capital commitment projection the sector has published. Its equally significant warning: future capacity growth will be "**constrained primarily by grid readiness rather than access to capital**," explicitly inverting the traditional infrastructure investment thesis. Capital scarcity no longer explains where data centres get built; power availability does.

The evidence arrived in the same week. **HSCALE** committed **€2B** across **250 MW** in Northwest Milan, choosing the site for proximity to Alpine grid transmission. **Nscale** closed a **$790M** debt facility for its **230 MW** Narvik campus powered by Norwegian municipal hydro at **€0.03–0.04/kWh**. **Digital Realty** launched its first **Barcelona** campus. Each was a power-first site decision — all three in markets outside FLAP-D (Frankfurt, London, Amsterdam, Paris, Dublin), where grid capacity is constrained and power costs are high.

## The Geography of Power

The power-cost differential is now a primary site selection variable. **Norway** (~€0.03–0.04/kWh hydro), **Sweden** (~€0.05/kWh), and Iberia (solar surplus) all offer **5–8× lower power costs** than UK industrial tariffs (~24.67p/kWh, approximately €0.29/kWh). **Ireland's CRU generation obligation** (Edition 10) now requires new data centre operators to build and operate matching generation capacity — converting power from a supply problem into a capital structure problem. These are not temporary imbalances; they reflect grid infrastructure built over decades that energy transition policy is only beginning to address.

For infrastructure investors, the EDCA forecast implies a two-segment market: legacy FLAP-D assets trade at a scarcity premium for contracted capacity that cannot be replicated, while new-build premium flows to power-surplus secondary markets. The strategic implication is that the most important policy decisions for European digital infrastructure competitiveness in the next five years are not AI regulation or spectrum auctions — they are electricity market reform, grid expansion permitting, and interconnector investment. That is a framing energy ministers have not yet internalised.

In the next 12–18 months, watch Germany's grid expansion plans, **Ofgem**'s resolution of the UK grid connection queue backlog, and whether any EU member state formally links its digital infrastructure strategy to power market design reform — that coupling, when it comes, will be the clearest signal that the constraint is being taken seriously.
articles.summary: EDCA forecast €176B in cumulative European data centre investment through 2031 while explicitly warning that power grid readiness — not capital — will determine where investment lands. The same week, HSCALE, Nscale, and Digital Realty all selected new European campus sites on power-first criteria, vindicating the forecast's central thesis.
